description_full: Build-A-Bear Workshop, Inc. operates as a mall-based, experiential specialty retailer for children in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, North America, and Europe. It operates through three segments: Direct-to-Consumer, Commercial, and International Franchising. The company offers various styles of plush products to be stuffed, pre-stuffed plush products, and sounds and scents that can be added to the stuffed animals, as well as range of clothing, shoes and accessories, and other toy and novelty items. It operates its stores under the Build-A-Bear Workshop brand name; and sells its products through its e-commerce sites and third-party marketplace sites. Build-A-Bear Workshop, Inc. was founded in 1997 and is headquartered in Saint Louis, Missouri.

financial_summary: Build-A-Bear Workshop, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $366M market cap on $530M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 65% against a 9% cost of capital — a 56-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 53% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $40M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.25× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 10.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 5.6% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 13% operating margin runs 5pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.54x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+8.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 46% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 59% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 57% and a beta of 0.94, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.54 vs 5y 0.89), so read it loosely.

val: The stock trades 54% below its DCF fair value of $65.22, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $52.95 to $82.35 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 7.4 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 6.7 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 9.3 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 21% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 10.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 14.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $45.00 on average, 52% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 65% clears the cost of capital of 9.4% by 56pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.70).
It runs a 53% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.25x.
ROE of 34% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 7pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $26.8M (7% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.2% over 3 years, 5.2% over 5 years and 3.8% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 16.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.6% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (4.8% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders own 5.6%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 10.7% a year to shareholders (7.6% in buybacks and 3.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 5.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 26.7% of the float, 5.9 days to cover.
people: With about 1,200 employees, each generates about $442K of revenue, 1.2x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $33K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $850K (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
